plan: Literary narrative (CLD-P-ACT-R-000061), an original story: a narrator helps an uncle count stock in his closing music shop and discovers a decades-long list of borrowed items, one returned. Narrator's gender unstated. Setting is a music shop, deliberately not a hardware store, to avoid CLD-P-ACT-R-000021 ('The Bottom Drawer', a hardware store before a sale). Ten questions, five aimed at hard (motive, contrast setup, combined-detail inference, understated dialogue, final image). Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: The Back Page
passages.text:
The week the music shop closed, my uncle Arno asked me to help him count everything. Not to sell it, he said. The new owners of the building would take the display cases, and a dealer from the city would take the stock. He only wanted to know what had been there.

So for five days I stood on the rolling ladder and read numbers down to him: forty-two packs of violin strings, eleven boxes of clarinet reeds, one accordion left from a polka craze nobody remembered. He wrote each number in a green ledger in handwriting so small and even it looked printed. When I asked why it mattered, since nobody was going to read the ledger, he said, "I'll read it," and went on writing.

On the fourth afternoon a man came in carrying a dented trumpet wrapped in a bath towel. He was only a few years younger than Arno, and he set the trumpet on the counter as if it might break. He had borrowed it, he said, in 1987, to play in his high school's spring concert, and had meant to bring it back the following Monday. He had heard the store was closing. He thought he had better hurry.

Arno unwrapped the trumpet and turned it over. I expected him to laugh, or to tell the man to keep it; it was a cheap student model, and its valves were stuck. Instead he opened the ledger to the back page, found a line I had not seen him write, and drew a neat stroke through it. Then he thanked the man, and the man left, and Arno went back to the numbers as if nothing had happened.

I climbed down from the ladder and looked at the back page. It was a list, in the same tiny hand, of things that had gone out the door and not come back: a cello, two flutes, a music stand, a trumpet. Each line had a name beside it and a date. Some were thirty years old. Only the trumpet had been crossed out.

"You kept track of all of these?" I asked.

"Somebody had to," he said. He did not look up. "People always mean to bring things back."

On the last day we locked the door at noon. Arno put the ledger under his arm, and he did not offer to let me carry it.

candidates.stem: Which of the following best describes what happens in the passage?

choices.A: The narrator persuades the uncle to keep the store open by showing how much stock remains.
choices.B: While counting a closing shop's stock, the narrator finds the uncle's record of trust.
choices.C: A customer returns a valuable instrument, and the uncle sells it to the dealer.
choices.D: The narrator and the uncle argue about whether the ledger should be kept.

candidates.evidence: things that had gone out the door and not come back
candidates.explanation: The narrator helps count the stock and discovers the back page, a long-kept list of borrowed items that reveals the uncle's lasting trust in customers.

A.rationale: The store closes as planned, and the narrator never tries to keep it open.

C.rationale: The trumpet is a cheap student model, and nothing suggests it is sold.

D.rationale: No argument occurs; the narrator only asks questions.

hints: What does the narrator discover on the back page?

strategy.explanation: Summarize the story's events in order.

candidates.remember: A main-event answer should include the story's turning point.

candidates.stem: Based on the passage, Arno most likely wants to count the stock because he:

choices.A: hopes to sell the stock himself for more than the dealer would pay.
choices.B: must give the new owners an exact list of the display cases.
choices.C: wants to teach the narrator how to manage a store in the future.
choices.D: wants a record of the store for himself, though no one else will use it.

candidates.evidence: He only wanted to know what had been there.
candidates.explanation: Arno says he only wants to know what had been there, and when asked who will read the ledger, he says, "I'll read it."

A.rationale: He says the count is "Not to sell it."

B.rationale: The new owners take the cases; nothing says they need a list.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests he is training the narrator for future work.

hints: What does Arno say when asked who will read the ledger?

strategy.explanation: Combine his two statements about the count.

candidates.remember: A character's own words often reveal motive.

author_checklist.hardness: The motive must be inferred from two brief statements; the distractors offer practical motives.

candidates.stem: The narrator's expectation that Arno would "laugh, or ... tell the man to keep it" (paragraph 4) mainly serves to:

choices.A: set up a contrast with Arno's careful response to the return.
choices.B: suggest that Arno was usually rude to customers.
choices.C: show that the narrator knew the trumpet had once been valuable.
choices.D: explain why the man had waited so long to return the trumpet.

candidates.evidence: Instead he opened the ledger to the back page
candidates.explanation: The narrator expects a casual reaction, but Arno instead crosses the item off his long-kept list, which reveals how much the return means to him.

B.rationale: Nothing in the passage shows Arno being rude.

C.rationale: The narrator thinks the trumpet is cheap.

D.rationale: The narrator's expectation concerns Arno's reaction, not the man's delay.

hints: What word follows the narrator's expectation?
candidates.remember: An expectation is often set up to be overturned.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must read the expectation as a setup for contrast rather than a fact about Arno.

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the word stroke most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: drew a neat stroke through it
candidates.explanation: Arno "drew a neat stroke" through a line in the ledger, so "stroke" means a line drawn with a pen.

A.rationale: A "blow" is a hit, which does not fit drawing in a ledger.

B.rationale: A caress is a gentle touch, not a mark on a page.

D.rationale: This medical sense does not fit drawing in a ledger.

hints: What do you draw through a line in a ledger?

strategy.explanation: Replace the word with a simple synonym.

candidates.remember: Choose the meaning that fits the action described.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the man borrowed the trumpet in order to:

choices.A: give lessons to students at the music shop.
choices.B: replace a dented trumpet of his own.
choices.C: play at Arno's store on its opening day.
choices.D: play in his high school's spring concert.

candidates.evidence: to play in his high school's spring concert
candidates.explanation: The man says he borrowed the trumpet in 1987 to play in his high school's spring concert.

A.rationale: He borrowed it to play in a concert, not to teach.

B.rationale: The passage gives no such reason.

C.rationale: Nothing connects the concert to the store's opening.

hints: Find the year 1987 in the passage.

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence with the year.

candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the exact sentence.

candidates.stem: The detail that "Only the trumpet had been crossed out" (paragraph 5) most strongly suggests that:

choices.A: Arno had forgotten to cross out other items when they were returned.
choices.B: most of the borrowed items on Arno's list were never returned.
choices.C: the trumpet was the most valuable item on the list.
choices.D: Arno had started the list only a few days before.

candidates.explanation: Arno keeps careful records, and only one of many items is crossed out, so the others were never returned, some after thirty years.

A.rationale: Arno records everything carefully, so forgetting is unlikely.

C.rationale: The narrator calls the trumpet a cheap student model.

D.rationale: Some entries were thirty years old.

hints: How careful is Arno's record keeping?

strategy.explanation: Combine the crossed-out detail with the ages of the entries.

candidates.remember: Combine details to draw an inference.

author_checklist.hardness: The inference depends on combining the crossed-out detail with Arno's careful habits.

candidates.stem: Arno's statement "People always mean to bring things back" most likely suggests that he:

choices.A: is angry that so many borrowers broke their promises.
choices.B: plans to contact each borrower and demand the items back.
choices.C: trusts borrowers' intentions even when items never return.
choices.D: regrets having lent instruments to his customers.

candidates.evidence: "People always mean to bring things back."
candidates.explanation: He describes borrowers by what they "mean" to do and keeps the list without pursuing them, which suggests generous faith rather than anger or regret.

A.rationale: He states the line calmly and keeps writing; nothing shows anger.

B.rationale: The store is closing, and nothing suggests he will pursue anyone.

D.rationale: Nothing in his words or actions shows regret.

hints: Is Arno's tone angry, regretful, or generous?

strategy.explanation: Read his actions alongside his words.

candidates.remember: Interpret a line using the character's tone and actions.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must read tone from understated dialogue rather than explicit statements.

candidates.stem: The passage is narrated from the point of view of:

choices.A: a relative who helped Arno during the store's final week.
choices.B: Arno, looking back on the day the store closed.
choices.C: the man who returned the trumpet.
choices.D: an outside narrator who knows each character's thoughts.

candidates.evidence: my uncle Arno asked me to help him
candidates.explanation: The narrator calls Arno "my uncle" and describes helping him during the store's last week.

B.rationale: The narrator speaks of "my uncle Arno," so Arno is not the narrator.

C.rationale: The man is described by the narrator, not narrating.

D.rationale: The narrator is a character who does not know Arno's thoughts.

candidates.remember: First-person narrators reveal themselves through relationships.

candidates.stem: The final sentence of the passage mainly suggests that Arno:

choices.A: does not trust the narrator to carry anything safely.
choices.B: plans to give the ledger to the dealer from the city.
choices.C: is relieved that the store has finally closed.
choices.D: treats the ledger as something personal to keep close.

candidates.evidence: he did not offer to let me carry it
candidates.explanation: Arno keeps the ledger under his arm and does not let anyone else carry it, which shows how personal the record is to him.

A.rationale: The narrator has helped all week; the detail is about the ledger, not distrust.

B.rationale: Nothing suggests he will give it away.

C.rationale: Nothing in the sentence shows relief.

hints: What has the passage shown about the ledger's importance to Arno?

strategy.explanation: Connect the last sentence to "I'll read it."

candidates.remember: Final images often echo a story's earlier details.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must connect the last image to Arno's earlier statement about reading the ledger.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, when did the narrator first see the list on the back page of the ledger?

choices.A: On the first day of counting, before any numbers were written
choices.B: After Arno crossed out the trumpet and the man left
choices.C: While reading numbers from the rolling ladder
choices.D: On the last day, after the door was locked

candidates.evidence: I climbed down from the ladder and looked at the back page
candidates.explanation: The narrator had not seen the line Arno crossed out, then climbed down and looked at the back page after the man left.

A.rationale: The narrator saw the back page only on the fourth afternoon.

C.rationale: The narrator climbed down from the ladder to look at the back page.

D.rationale: The narrator saw the list on the fourth afternoon, before the last day.

hints: Find where the narrator climbs down from the ladder.

strategy.explanation: Trace the order of events on the fourth afternoon.

candidates.remember: Sequence questions need the order of events, not just the events.
